Chapter 3: Deciding What to Keep and What to Let Go
At the heart of death cleaning, everything comes down to the choices we make about our possessions. This isn’t just a practical step—it’s a personal journey, where logic and emotion have to find their balance. And the real question isn’t just, “Is this useful?”—it’s, “Does this actually matter to me right now?”
Here’s a tip that can really help: picture the people who might one day sort through your things. Would they understand why you kept that old ticket stub, or would it just leave them scratching their heads? Would the item bring them a smile, or just create more work—or even a little discomfort? Putting yourself in their shoes can make it a lot clearer what’s truly worth holding onto, and what it’s time to release.
When it comes to sorting, it helps to break things down into a few simple categories:
There are the things you’ll keep and keep using. Some items are perfect for gifting to family or friends. Others might be better off donated or sold. And then there’s the stuff you can simply recycle or toss.
Now, sentimental items can be the trickiest. It’s important to notice the difference between things that spark positive memories and those that just weigh on your heart without serving you anymore. Think about a box of old letters or photos. Sure, some are treasures, but do you really need the duplicates or the ones that don’t mean much anymore? The idea isn’t to erase the past, but to keep a collection of memories that’s both manageable and meaningful.
Heirlooms and family treasures deserve a little extra care. These are more than just objects—they’re stories and connections that reach beyond you. Sharing their history with loved ones can turn the act of giving into a special moment, instead of just handing something over. Ask yourself, will the person receiving this appreciate it and look after it? Or maybe it would find a better home somewhere else?
There are some practical questions that can guide your decisions:
Have you actually used or appreciated this item in the past year? Does it fit your life and your space as it is right now? When you pick it up, how does it make you feel—do you light up, or just shrug? And if someone else ended up with it, how do you imagine they’d react?
Letting go isn’t always easy, especially when things are tied to big moments or cherished relationships. It’s totally normal to feel a wave of loss or nostalgia. But here’s the thing—releasing what you no longer need can bring a sense of relief and freedom. It’s not about giving up, it’s about making space for what truly matters to you.
By choosing carefully what stays and what goes, you’re crafting a living space that really reflects your values and priorities. In the end, curating your possessions is a form of self-expression—and it shapes the legacy you leave behind, making it both manageable and meaningful for those who follow.
